original_question: Let f: [0, 1] → c_0 be bounded, and let I(f) denote the set of all limits of sequences of Riemann sums of f taken over partitions whose diameters tend to 0. Must I(f) always be convex?
target_in_paper: Problem 3.3 (Kadets-Kadets) in §3.1, “Riemann integral”: for bounded f:[0,1]→c0, is the limit set I(f) of Riemann sums convex? ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s exact target very closely: it uses the correct interval [0,1], the correct codomain c0, the correct boundedness assumption, the correct limit-set notation I(f), and the exact convexity question posed in Problem 3.3. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper works throughout with real Banach spaces, so c0 should be understood as the real Banach space of null sequences with its usual sup norm unless stated otherwise. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))

To make the question fully stand-alone, I(f) should be defined using tagged finite partitions P=(0=t0<...<tm=1; ξi∈[t_{i-1},t_i]) and the corresponding Riemann sums Σ_i f(ξi)(t_i-t_{i-1}); the paper refers to this only through the standard phrase about limits of Riemann sums over partitions whose diameter tends to 0. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))

The function f is only assumed bounded, not necessarily Riemann integrable; that point is explicit in the sentence introducing I(f). ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
The diameter/mesh condition should be stated explicitly as max_i(t_i-t_{i-1})→0. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))

The paper’s unresolved case is specifically c0, not an arbitrary Banach space X; a refined version should not broaden the question beyond c0. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))

In the specific case X=c0, the nearby context implies I(f) is already known to be nonempty because I(f)≠∅ whenever X is separable; this is useful hidden context if one wants the question to read as substantively as it does in the paper. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
refined_question: Let c0 be the real Banach space of all real sequences converging to 0, with the sup norm, and let f:[0,1]→c0 be a bounded function, not assumed Riemann integrable. For a tagged finite partition P=(0=t0<...<tm=1; ξi∈[t_{i-1},t_i]) of [0,1], define the Riemann sum S(f,P)=Σ_{i=1}^m f(ξi)(t_i-t_{i-1}) and the mesh ||P||=max_i(t_i-t_{i-1}). Set I(f)={x∈c0: there exists a sequence of tagged partitions Pn of [0,1] with ||Pn||→0 and S(f,Pn)→x in c0}. Must I(f) be a convex subset of c0 for every bounded function f:[0,1]→c0? ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
justification: This is the paper’s exact open problem, not a neighboring generalization. In §3.1 the author first introduces I(f) for a bounded f:[0,1]→X as the set of limits of sequences of Riemann sums over partitions whose diameter tends to 0, notes that I(f) is known to be nonempty for separable X and convex for super-reflexive X, and then specializes the unresolved question to X=c0 in Problem 3.3. The notation section also fixes the ambient scalar field to real Banach spaces. Your draft is therefore essentially correct, but a paper-faithful stand-alone formulation should spell out the tagged-partition/Riemann-sum convention and the mesh condition explicitly, and mention that no Riemann integrability of f is assumed. ([webs.um.es](https://webs.um.es/joserr/miwiki/lib/exe/fetch.php?cache=cache&id=papers&media=openproblems.pdf))
